growth_story.headline: Djibouti's income per person has grown 4.1 percent a year since 2014 on ports and a railway serving Ethiopia, leaving high debt and few formal jobs.
growth_story.arc: The data show one era from 2014 to 2025, with income per person growing 4.1 percent a year and no lasting break. The early years ran at 5.3 to 5.5 percent as Djibouti built new ports, a railway and a water pipeline to Ethiopia, largely with borrowed money, and investment reached 30.3 percent of GDP in 2015. Growth then eased, to 3.1 percent in 2018, and dipped to -0.3 percent in 2020, the year of COVID-19, before recovering to 3.7 percent in 2022 through shocks that included the Tigray crisis in Ethiopia. From 2023 it picked up again, to 5.3, 5.5 and 5.1 percent, helped in 2024 by a surge in transshipment as ships rerouted around Red Sea tensions. Income per person reached its highest level so far in 2025, but the IMF and World Bank say the build-out left heavy debt and that growth has created few jobs.

threads.title: Building a port for Ethiopia
threads.text: Over the past decade Djibouti built new ports, a railway and a water pipeline to Ethiopia, making itself the main port for its large neighbor. Investment rose from 25.0 percent of GDP in 2013 to 30.3 percent in 2015, and income per person grew 5.3 to 5.5 percent a year in 2014 to 2016.

citations.quote: The development of new ports and high-quality infrastructure—including a railway and a water pipeline to Ethiopia—has propelled average growth rates to about 6 percent

threads.title: Shocks from next door
threads.text: Growth slowed after the build-out, to 3.1 percent in 2018, and dipped to -0.3 percent in 2020, the year of COVID-19. The authorities name COVID-19, the 2022 Tigray crisis in Ethiopia and the Ukraine war among the shocks of recent years; income per person grew 2.9 percent in 2021 and 3.7 percent in 2022. The sources say little more about why these years were slower.

citations.title: Djibouti: 2025 Article IV Consultation-Press Release and Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 25/276)
citations.quote: Djibouti has successfully navigated several shocks in recent years, including COVID-19, the 2022 Tigray crisis, the Ukraine war

threads.title: Red Sea detours and Ethiopian demand
threads.text: Income per person grew 5.3, 5.5 and 5.1 percent in 2023 to 2025. In 2024 transshipment at Djibouti's ports surged as shipping rerouted around Red Sea tensions. The Ethiopia corridor remains a main source of trade, which ties Djibouti's growth to its neighbor's demand.

citations.title: Djibouti: 2025 Article IV Consultation-Press Release and Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 25/276)
citations.quote: The increase in port activity was dominated by a 98 percent surge in transshipments, as shipping operators rerouted to circumvent Red Sea tensions

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Djibouti (October 2026)
citations.quote: The Ethiopia corridor has been a main source of trade but also ties Djibouti's fortunes to its neighbor's demand.

threads.title: Debt from the build-out
threads.text: The ports, railway and pipeline were paid for largely with loans, so public debt rose steeply. The IMF judged Djibouti to be in debt distress in 2025, and in 2026 the World Bank said the debt still needed restructuring.

citations.title: Djibouti: 2025 Article IV Consultation-Press Release and Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 25/276)
citations.quote: Debt-to-GDP increased from 34.9 percent in 2013 to 68.9 percent by the end of 2024. This rise was primarily driven by major infrastructure projects

citations.title: Djibouti: 2025 Article IV Consultation-Press Release and Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 25/276)
citations.quote: Djibouti remains in debt distress, and debt is deemed unsustainable.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Djibouti (October 2026)
citations.quote: debt restructuring is still required to curb high debt service needs in the short term.

threads.title: Growth with few jobs
threads.text: Growth built on ports and logistics has not brought many jobs. Djibouti's first labor force survey, in 2025, found more than half of working-age people outside the labor force, with unemployment highest among young people and women.

citations.title: Djibouti: 2025 Article IV Consultation-Press Release and Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 25/276)
citations.quote: Despite high growth, fewer than one third of the working-age population are formally employed.

since_last_year.text: Growth held up in 2025 on strong port activity, though transshipment fell back from 2024; income per person grew 5.1 percent. In 2026 renewed insecurity in the Red Sea raised freight and insurance costs, and the World Bank cut its 2026 forecast. A new National Development Plan for 2025-30, adopted in February 2026, aims to move the economy beyond trade and logistics.

growth_story.tension: The IMF says growth of about 6 percent a year doubled GDP per capita between 2013 and 2023. In the data, income per person rose from about 2,140 in 2013 to about 3,118 in 2023, well short of doubling, and grew 3.8 percent a year over 2016 to 2025. The sources give whole-economy growth rates and do not say how much of the gap comes from population growth or from a different data series.
